units.text: Departure from Mecca: The Plan, the Bed, and the Entrusted Property
What does Ibn Ishaq relate about Quraysh’s council and the Prophet’s bed where Ali slept, and what does Urwa relate about the departure by night?
The journey begins with waiting for permission in Mecca and Quraysh’s fear that the Prophet ﷺ would leave; Ali then slept on the Prophet’s bed and remained behind to return the entrusted property.
Before the departure

When the emigrants left, the Prophet ﷺ remained in Mecca awaiting permission, as Ibn Ishaq relates, and Ali and Abu Bakr stayed with him. Abu Bakr repeatedly sought permission to leave, but the Prophet ﷺ told him not to hurry. In this account, the possibility of companionship thus remained open, without any set date of departure.

According to Ibn Ishaq's narrative, Quraysh saw that the emigrants had found a home and protection outside Mecca and feared that the Prophet ﷺ would join them. They met at Dar al-Nadwa to discuss what to do about him.
The consultation and the plan

In Ibn Abbas’s account as related by Ibn Ishaq, one proposal is to imprison the Prophet ﷺ; the Najdi elder rejects it. A different proposal is to exile him, which the elder also rejects. Abu Jahl then proposes giving a sword to a young man from each tribe so that they can strike the Prophet ﷺ together in one blow and kill him. His reasoning is that responsibility for the blood would be spread among the tribes, leaving Banu Abd Manaf unable to fight them all. In this account the council settles on Abu Jahl’s plan.

This route of transmission includes mention of Iblis in the guise of an elder. Al-Suwayani reports that the account is strengthened by its routes in one place, but elsewhere excludes the mention of Iblis.
The bed and the doorway

In the account from Ibn Abbas, the Prophet ﷺ is warned not to spend the night on the bed where he usually slept, and watchers gather at his door. He instructs Ali to sleep on his bed, cover himself with his green Hadrami cloak, and assures him that nothing he dislikes will reach him from them.

In another account related by Ibn Ishaq from Yazid ibn Ziyad from Muhammad ibn Kab al-Qurazi, Abu Jahl stands with the men at the door. The Prophet ﷺ then comes out to them, scatters dust, and recites verses from Surat Ya-Sin. The men look toward the bed, see the person covered by the cloak and think it is the Prophet ﷺ, until Ali rises in the morning and they realize who was there.
The entrusted property, then joining him

In Ibn Ishaq's other report, Ali's task was not merely to sleep on the bed. In an explicitly marked report of what had reached him, Ibn Ishaq says the Prophet ﷺ told Ali of his departure and ordered him to stay behind to return people's entrusted property.

Later in the narrative, Ali stayed in Mecca for three nights and their days until he had returned the entrusted property; then he joined the Prophet ﷺ and lodged with him at the home of Kulthum ibn Hidm.
Departure by night and the watchers at the house

Al-Bayhaqi transmits from Urwa ibn al-Zubayr a shorter picture of the plot: killing, imprisonment, expulsion or binding, along with a verse from al-Anfal, the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr departing at night toward the cave, and Ali lying on the bed. Urwa’s report does not mention the Dar al-Nadwa dialogue or the scattering of earth; the verse of al-Anfal there is Qur’anic text, not a continuation of the council’s dialogue.
Urwa’s report mentions departing at night, while Ibn Abbas’s report places the watchers at the Prophet’s ﷺ door in the darkness. Neither gives the hour of the separate visit to Abu Bakr’s house.
What do the critics' assessments say?

A note by al-Suwayani says the report about the council is hasan through its various routes; he calls the route through al-Kalbi unsatisfactory, describes al-Hasan ibn Umara as abandoned, and mentions a corroborating mursal report from Qatada and the abandoned transmitter al-Waqidi. In another text, he excludes the mention of Iblis from his favorable assessment of the hadith.

Al-Suwayani discusses a route through Abu Balj. He says its chain is acceptable provided Abu Balj is not alone in transmitting contradictory wording. He mentions both endorsements by some scholars and al-Bukhari’s criticism «فيه نظر» (fīhi naẓar); al-Suwayani describes al-Bukhari’s technical expression as severe.

In Ibn Ishaq’s account, the Prophet ﷺ tells Ali to cover himself with the green Hadrami cloak. Ibn Ishaq relates the scattering of earth and recitation of Ya-Sin through Yazid ibn Ziyad from Muhammad ibn Ka‘b al-Qurazi.
Mecca addressed at al-Hazwara

In a report transmitted by al-Bayhaqi from Abdullah ibn Adi ibn al-Hamra, the Prophet ﷺ addresses Mecca while standing at al-Hazwara in its market: it is the best of God’s lands and the dearest to him, and he would not have left it had he not been driven out. Al-Bayhaqi regards this version as preserved. The report gives no hour for his standing at al-Hazwara and does not link it to the door of the Prophet’s ﷺ house or to the Prophet’s bed on which Ali slept.
In his discussion of the Hazwara report, al-Bayhaqi calls Ma‘mar’s variant mistaken. He separately calls what some transmitted from Muhammad ibn Amr mistaken and prefers the group’s version.

Why did the Prophet ﷺ remain in Mecca after his companions, according to Ibn Ishaq?
Ibn Ishaq relates that he was waiting for permission, while Ali and Abu Bakr remained in Mecca after the other emigrants.
The period of waiting in Mecca in Ibn Ishaq's account.
To await permission to emigrate
Ibn Ishaq states that he remained in Mecca awaiting permission to emigrate.
Because he had already reached Quba
Quba appears in the later report of Ali joining him, not as a reason for the Prophet ﷺ to remain in Mecca.
Which plan did the Quraysh council settle on in the account from Ibn Abbas?
Abu Jahl links the tribes' joint action to the dispersal of responsibility for bloodshed among them; the text reports the Najdi elder's approval and the men's parting in agreement on this plan.
The conclusion within Ibn Abbas's account of the council, not a judgment that every detail of the council is established.
Postponing the matter until another season
The report does not mention postponement until a season; it ends with a plan to kill him involving the tribes.
Young men from the tribes joining in the killing
After proposals to imprison and exile him, Abu Jahl proposes that young men from the tribes strike him together in a single blow.
What exception does al-Suwayani mention in his assessment of the report about the Najdi shaykh?
Al-Suwayani's favorable assessment of the report through its routes is qualified by his exception of the mention of Iblis; he discusses some of its routes and corroborating reports in detail.
An assessment attributed to al-Suwayani, not an independent ruling on the underlying report.
Mention al-Suwayani's exception to his assessment
Al-Suwayani explicitly excludes the mention of Iblis from his favorable assessment of the report.
Assert that all critics authenticated it
Al-Suwayani's exception for Iblis contradicts extending his authentication to every detail and every critic.
Which chain does Ibn Ishaq explicitly give for the account of scattering dust?
The chain for the dust account begins with Ibn Ishaq saying that Yazid ibn Ziyad told him on the authority of Muhammad ibn Kab al-Qurazi; it is not a continuation of the route from Ibn Abbas.
The order of this report's chain as shown in the first part of the reading.
Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Abbas ← Yazid ibn Ziyad
This choice conflates the two routes and attributes the account to Ibn Abbas; here Ibn Ishaq begins a different chain through Yazid ibn Ziyad from Muhammad ibn Kab.
Ibn Ishaq ← Yazid ibn Ziyad ← Muhammad ibn Kab al-Qurazi
Ibn Ishaq's account states: “Yazid ibn Ziyad told me, from Muhammad ibn Kab al-Qurazi, who said:”.
What does Urwa's brief account say about Ali?
Urwa's account brings together the forms of the plot, departure toward the cave, and Ali's lying on the bed, without Abu Jahl's detailed dialogue.
The reference is to the account of Urwa presented here, not all reports of the departure.
He lay on the Prophet's ﷺ bed
Urwa mentions Ali's lying on the Prophet's ﷺ bed at the end of his brief account.
Abu Jahl's dialogue with everyone present at the council
The detail of Abu Jahl's words at the door belongs to the report from Muhammad ibn Kab, not Urwa's shorter selection.
What qualification did Ibn Ishaq explicitly give in the report about the entrusted property?
The preserved formula “as it reached me” (fima balaghani) is an unsourced report from Ibn Ishaq; it must not be converted into the name of an omitted transmitter.
The qualification about transmission in the selection on entrusted property.
A named chain of direct hearing in the same passage
Had Ibn Ishaq named a transmitter for the entrusted property here, he would not have said that the report reached him in this form.
“As it reached me” (fima balaghani)
The text repeats “as it reached me” (fima balaghani) when mentioning that Ali was told of the departure and instructed to return the entrusted property.
When does the account of the entrusted property say that Ali joined him?
The report says Ali finished returning the entrusted property and then joined the Prophet ﷺ and lodged with him at the home of Kulthum ibn Hidm.
The sequence of the report about the property and Ali's joining him, not an hour-by-hour timing of the departure.
After returning the entrusted property
The text links Ali's joining him to his completion of the task of returning the property for which he had stayed behind.
Before sleeping on the bed
This text does not place Ali's joining him before the night of the bed; rather, it mentions his remaining in Mecca for three nights and their days.
What condition did al-Suwayani place on his assessment of the route through Abu Balj?
Al-Suwayani cites both endorsements and criticism of Abu Balj, then qualifies his assessment of the chain by the absence of a wording that Abu Balj transmits alone in contradiction to others.
The cited judgment is specific to the route and wording under discussion.
Rejecting all reports about Ali without exception
The discussion of the route through Abu Balj does not invalidate every report about Ali or all their wordings.
That he not be alone in transmitting contradictory wording
Al-Suwayani's phrase “there is no problem with it” is qualified by the condition that Abu Balj not be alone in transmitting contradictory wording.
Where does the address expressing love for Mecca appear in this chapter?
The al-Hazwara report relates the Prophet's ﷺ standing in the Meccan market and addressing Mecca, followed by al-Bayhaqi's comment on the preserved version.
Al-Hazwara is the place of the report, not a timestamp for the scene at the bed.
In the al-Hazwara report from Ibn Adi ibn al-Hamra
Abdullah ibn Adi ibn al-Hamra relates the Prophet's ﷺ words addressed to Mecca at al-Hazwara.
In Abu Jahl's proposal at the council
Abu Jahl's proposal concerns a plan to kill him, not the Prophet's ﷺ words about his love for Mecca.
How did al-Bayhaqi describe certain other narrations in the context of al-Hazwara?
Al-Bayhaqi calls the two routes he names mistaken and prefers the group's version; he does not apply this judgment to every departure account.
Al-Bayhaqi's preference among forms of the al-Hazwara report in the context of his text.
As specifying the hour of an encounter at the bed
Al-Bayhaqi identifies errors in the mentioned routes, not the hour of an encounter at the bed.
As mistaken, while preferring the group's version
Al-Bayhaqi mentions an error by Mamar and the route through Muhammad ibn Amr, then prefers the group's version.

The cited criticism of the route through Abu Balj is qualified. The text of the report al-Suwayani discussed was not extracted within this assignment, so this criticism cannot establish its details or negate all accounts about Ali.

Ibn Ishaq said: When Quraysh saw that the Messenger of God ﷺ had acquired supporters and companions from outside their own people in a land other than their own, and saw his emigrant companions leaving to join them, they realized that they had settled in a home and found protection among them. They feared the Messenger of God ﷺ might go to join them, and understood that there was a resolve to wage war against them. [Translator’s note: The supplied Arabic has plural “annahum” beside singular “ajmaʿa”; the subject of the resolve is uncertain.] So they gathered to discuss him in the House of Assembly—this was the house of Qusayy ibn Kilab, where Quraysh settled all their affairs—to consult about what to do with the Messenger of God ﷺ now that they feared him.

Some said to the others, “You have seen what has become of this man. By God, we cannot feel safe from his attacking us with those outside our people who have followed him. Agree on a plan for dealing with him.” They consulted, and one of them said, “Put him in irons, lock a door on him, then wait for the fate that befell poets like him who came before—Zuhayr, al-Nabigha, and those who have passed away: death—until it befalls him too [3].” The Najdi elder said, “No, by God, this is not a sound plan for you. By God, if you imprison him as you say, news of his cause will surely pass from behind the door you have locked—

Then one of them said, “Let us drive him from among us and banish him from our land. Once he is gone, by God, we will not care where he goes or where he ends up. With him absent and ourselves rid of him, we can set our affairs right and restore our harmony as it was [1].” The Najdi elder said, “No, by God, this is not a sound plan for you. Have you not seen how fine his speech is, how appealing his words are, and how he wins men's hearts with what he brings? By God, if you do that, you cannot be sure he will not settle among an Arab tribe, win them over with his words until they follow him, then march with them against you, trample you in your own land, seize control of your affairs and do to you what he wishes. Devise [2] a different plan for him.”

He said: Abu Jahl ibn Hisham said, “By God, I have a plan for him that I do not think you have hit upon yet.” They asked, “What is it, Abu al-Hakam?” He said, “I propose that we take from each tribe a young, hardy man of respected lineage and standing [3] among us and give each a sharp sword. Then they should go to him and strike him together as one man, killing him and relieving us of him. For if they do so, responsibility for his blood will be spread among all the tribes. Banu Abd Manaf will be unable to fight all their people, and will accept blood money from us, which we will pay them.” The Najdi elder said, “What this man has said is the right plan; there is no other.” The men parted in agreement on it.

(2) A hadith assessed as hasan through its routes. Ibn Ishaq related it, and al-Tabari (2/370) related it through him by several routes in which Ibn Ishaq explicitly reported having heard it, including from al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. This route is not one to welcome, because it contains al-Kalbi, who is severely discredited. As for the second route, it is al-Hasan ibn Umara from al-Hakam ibn Utayba from Miqsam from Ibn Abbas; al-Hasan is abandoned as a transmitter. As for the third route, its men are trustworthy: “Abdullah ibn Abi Najih told me, from Mujahid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas.” Mujahid is a well-known trustworthy leading Successor, and Abdullah ibn Abi Najih is trustworthy, though he may sometimes practice tadlis, that is, he does so rarely. The hadith has corroborating reports that undoubtedly make it hasan: Abd al-Razzaq related it with a sound chain from Qatada (5/389), as a mursal report, and that is a sufficient corroboration. It has another corroboration through al-Waqidi, with several chains from Ali, Aisha and Suraqa. Al-Waqidi is abandoned as a transmitter.
